analysis.one_liner: Removes the income cap on ACA premium subsidies and makes the enlarged subsidies permanent.
analysis.headline: A bill with 45 Senate cosponsors, including the Majority Leader and the Finance Committee chair, never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code so that anyone buying an ACA marketplace plan can get a premium tax credit, no matter how high their income — today the credit disappears entirely above about four times the poverty level. It would also shrink the share of income families at every income level must pay for coverage and make these bigger credits permanent starting in 2026. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Households who buy their own health insurance through the ACA marketplaces. Families earning above about four times the poverty level (roughly $125,000 for a family of four) would become eligible for the first time, with premiums capped at 8.5% of income. Families below that line would pay a smaller share of their income for the same coverage, with the help shrinking on a sliding scale as income rises.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 400%-of-poverty income cap so households of any income buying marketplace coverage can qualify for a premium tax credit, capped at 8.5% of their income.
Deepens the credits at every income tier — for example, a family between 200% and 250% of poverty would pay 2% to 4% of income in premiums instead of roughly 6% to 8.5%.
Strikes the disqualifiers tied to the old income cap, including the rules that barred people above 400% of poverty from receiving any credit at all.
Makes the expanded credits permanent by applying them to all tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, with no expiration date.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill contains no tax increases or spending offsets, so the expanded credits would be financed entirely by higher federal deficits. Marketplace insurers also benefit, since they gain a larger, permanently subsidized customer base — the subsidies flow through private insurance plans rather than a public option.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes no pay-fors: it lifts the income cap and deepens the credits with no offsetting taxes or cuts, so the entire cost lands on federal deficits.
Removing the 400% income cap extends subsidies to higher-income households who could otherwise afford coverage, which is the costliest and least-targeted part of the expansion.
The credits are made permanent with no expiration or review, locking in open-ended federal spending through private insurance plans indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The affordability help is real and large: families buying their own coverage would see premiums drop materially, and the hated 'subsidy cliff' — where a small raise above the income line meant losing thousands of dollars in help — would end. The honest cost is fiscal: an uncapped, permanent, unsubsidized-by-offsets expansion of premium credits is expensive, and independent estimates of extending the enhanced credits run to the hundreds of billions of dollars over a decade. A more targeted design could have helped lower-income families sooner while phasing out help at high incomes more steeply.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The Health Care Affordability Act of 2024 was introduced in the Senate on September 25, 2024, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
Forty-five senators cosponsored the bill — 44 of the 48 Senate Democrats plus one independent — including Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and Finance Committee Chair Ron Wyden.
The bill received no further action: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because the bill was never enacted, the enhanced marketplace credits in current law were left scheduled to run only through the end of 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of new federal health spending came out ahead, since no expansion was enacted and the scheduled end of the enhanced credits stood. Marketplace insurers keep their existing subsidized customer base through 2025 but face uncertainty about the larger permanent customer base the bill would have locked in.

for.name: Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end the ACA subsidy income cap and make the enhanced credits permanent.

for.name: 44 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from nearly the entire Democratic caucus.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but as committee chair never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored or supported the bill, which expanded ACA subsidies the party had opposed extending; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill had no path even if the Senate had acted.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents — 44 of 48 Senate Democrats plus one independent — and no Republican signed on; there was never a roll-call vote to show a fuller split.

industries.note: The bill routes the expanded premium credits through private marketplace plans, permanently enlarging insurers' subsidized customer base and locking in their role as the channel for federal help with coverage. Ordinary people get cheaper premiums at the same time, so the industry's gain and the public's gain run together — though the money flows through insurers rather than a public plan.

industries.industry: Households above 400% of the poverty line
industries.note: Removing the income cap makes these higher-income households newly eligible for premium credits, capped at 8.5% of income, paid for by the federal treasury.
